mcqs.q: “Behavioral science” is best defined as the study of human behavior at the level of:
opts: The self, other individuals, family & community — and its effect on dental-health programs
mcqs.explain: Behavioral science studies human behavior at the level of the self, individuals, family and community, and the resulting reaction on dental-health programs.

mcqs.q: Psychology is defined as the study of human behaviour — specifically:
opts: How people behave and WHY they behave the way they do
mcqs.explain: Psychology = the study of human behaviour: how people behave and why they behave in just the way they do.

mcqs.q: Which branch is concerned with how and why perceptions, attitudes and behavior vary across different groups and societies?
mcqs.explain: Social psychology deals with individuals living in society/groups and how/why perceptions, thoughts, opinions, attitudes and behavior vary across groups.

mcqs.q: The process through which society influences individuals — so that we internalize others' attitudes as our own — is called:
mcqs.explain: Socialization is the process through which society influences individuals; we tend to internalize the attitudes of those around us.

mcqs.q: “Health behaviour” is any activity undertaken to promote, protect or maintain health:
opts: Whether or not it is objectively effective toward that end
Only if proven effective by a trial
Only when prescribed by a dentist
Only in patients with chronic disease
mcqs.explain: Health behaviour is any activity undertaken to promote/protect/maintain health, whether or not such behaviour is objectively effective toward that end (Health Promotion Glossary, 1986).

mcqs.q: A key reason to study behavioral dentistry is that populations are increasingly:
opts: Heterogeneous and migrating, bringing different cultural expectations
mcqs.explain: Populations are becoming increasingly heterogeneous and migrating longer distances, bringing different cultural expectations and needs that affect management of oro-dental disease.

mcqs.q: Acknowledging the many ‘determinants of health’ allows the professional to:
opts: Work WITH the patient to find the individual path to optimal wellness
mcqs.explain: Recognising the variety of influences on health lets the professional work with the patient to understand the individual approach for optimal wellness.

mcqs.q: From the PATIENT's perspective, which is a recognised behavioral problem?
opts: Poor drug compliance and lack of awareness of one's disease status
mcqs.explain: Patient-perspective problems include poor drug compliance, special-needs issues, emotional instability and lack of awareness of disease status or self-image.

mcqs.q: In Corah's survey, which was rated a principal patient behavioral problem from the DENTIST's perspective?
mcqs.explain: Dentists listed fee collection, fearful patients, poor home-care motivation, not following instructions, poorly behaved children, and broken/cancelled/late appointments.

mcqs.q: Educational theory recognises how many domains of learning?
mcqs.explain: There are three domains of learning: cognitive, affective and behavioral.

mcqs.q: The COGNITIVE domain of learning is concerned with:
opts: Acquiring factual knowledge & intellectual understanding of ideas
mcqs.explain: The cognitive domain refers to acquisition of factual knowledge and intellectual understanding of ideas.

mcqs.q: Attitudes, beliefs and values belong to which domain of learning?
mcqs.explain: The affective domain is concerned with attitudes, beliefs and values.

mcqs.q: The BEHAVIORAL domain of learning refers to:
mcqs.explain: The behavioural domain refers to the skill or actions performed.

mcqs.q: The traditional ‘KAB’ model of dental health education assumes that:
opts: Knowledge changes Attitudes, which changes Behavior
Behavior must change before any knowledge is given
Attitudes are fixed and cannot change
mcqs.explain: The KAB model assumes acquiring new knowledge alters attitudes and leads to behavior change; in reality a complex, dynamic relationship operates between the three domains.

mcqs.q: In reality, the relationship between the three domains of learning is:
opts: Complex and dynamic — knowledge alone rarely changes behavior
mcqs.explain: A very complex and dynamic relationship operates between the three domains; the simple linear KAB assumption does not hold.

mcqs.q: Historically, the dental clinician–patient roles were characterised as:
mcqs.explain: Clinicians were cast as ‘active, powerful, expert’ and patients as ‘passive, cooperative’; the treatment room reinforces these roles.

mcqs.q: ‘Adoption’ of a health behavior change refers to its:
mcqs.explain: Adoption = acceptance of the care/behavior change; integration = its practical application — both need further exploration for success.

mcqs.q: ‘Integration’ of a behavior change refers to its:
opts: Practical application into the patient's lifestyle
mcqs.explain: Integration is the practical application of the care or behavior change; adoption is the acceptance step that precedes it.

mcqs.q: Underestimating communication relative to technical skill tends to foster a focus on:
mcqs.explain: Many oral-health professionals underestimate communication versus technical skill, fostering a focus on compliance rather than collaboration.

mcqs.q: What makes the dental clinician–patient relationship uniquely suited to behavior change?
opts: Its nature, frequency and longevity, unlike any other health-care setting
mcqs.explain: The nature, frequency and longevity of the dental interaction is unlike any other health-care environment, giving a limitless opportunity to build positive behaviors.

mcqs.q: Which statement about behavior change is TRUE?
opts: It requires effort and is seldom comfortable, easy or convenient
It is effortless once knowledge is given
It never involves the patient's environment
mcqs.explain: Behavior change requires effort, involves new habits/choices, and no single approach guarantees success — it can be a struggle for patient and clinician.

mcqs.q: Theories of health behavior differ mainly in their emphasis on:
mcqs.explain: Some theories emphasise individual factors (cognitions, emotions); others include environmental factors such as socio-economic status or family influence.

mcqs.q: From the patient's perspective, which is one of the five behavior-change concepts?
opts: Change can happen naturally in everyday life
mcqs.explain: Patient-perspective concepts: change can happen naturally; intrinsic motivation matters; readiness; ambivalence; and change happens in the context of the patient's life.

mcqs.q: Which type of motivation is highlighted as affecting patient behavior?
mcqs.explain: Intrinsic motivation affects patient behavior; it is one of the five patient-perspective concepts of working with behavior change.

mcqs.q: “People change when they are ready” expresses the concept of:
mcqs.explain: Readiness — people change when they are ready — is a core concept in working with behavior change.

mcqs.q: ‘Ambivalence’ in behavior change means:
opts: Feeling two ways about something — a normal part of the process
mcqs.explain: Ambivalence (feeling two ways about something) is part of the change process, on both the patient's and clinician's side.

mcqs.q: A dental clinician may have how long in a typical consultation to discuss behavior change?
mcqs.explain: In any consultation you may have as little as 5 or 10 minutes to discuss changes the patient could make to improve oral health.

mcqs.q: Which is identified as a KEY clinical tool / interpersonal skill for behavior change?
mcqs.explain: Interpersonal skills — particularly empathy — are a key clinical tool from the clinician's perspective.

mcqs.q: From the clinician's perspective, one listed pitfall is the limitation of:
mcqs.explain: The clinician's five keys include the limitations of giving advice and of a “fix-it” approach, plus the role of ambivalence, empathy, and agreeing on priorities.

mcqs.q: A patient who finds a very minor flaw so repellent that they avoid leaving the house, and repeatedly seeks cosmetic dental work, may have:
mcqs.explain: BDD: the physical abnormality is minor but the concern is clearly excessive; such patients often seek cosmetic interventions — remain vigilant and practice restraint.

saqs.q: Define behavioral science, psychology and social psychology.
saqs.a: Behavioral science = the study of human behavior at the level of the self, individuals, family & community, and its resulting reaction on dental-health programs. Psychology = the study of human behaviour — how people behave and why. Social psychology = the psychology of individuals in society/groups, studying how & why perceptions, attitudes and behavior vary across groups.

saqs.q: Name the three domains of learning and what each is concerned with.
saqs.a: Cognitive = acquiring factual knowledge & intellectual understanding of ideas. Affective = attitudes, beliefs and values. Behavioral = the skill or actions performed.

saqs.q: Explain the KAB model and why it is considered too simple.
saqs.a: The KAB model assumes new Knowledge alters Attitudes which leads to a change in Behavior. It is too simple because, in reality, a complex and dynamic relationship operates between the three domains — knowledge alone rarely changes behavior.

saqs.q: List four behavioral problems of patients from the dentist's perspective.
saqs.a: Any four of: fee collection; fearful patients; poor motivation for home care/plaque control; ignoring benefits of preventive care; not following instructions; insurance paperwork; poorly behaved children; broken/cancelled/late appointments; demands for unnecessary extractions; seeking only emergency care; parental neglect of children's teeth.

saqs.q: List the five behavior-change concepts from the patient's perspective.
saqs.a: 1) Change can happen naturally in everyday life. 2) Intrinsic motivation affects behavior. 3) People change when they are ready (readiness). 4) Ambivalence (feeling two ways) is part of the process. 5) Change happens in the context of the patient's life.

saqs.q: What is body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) and how should the dentist respond?
saqs.a: BDD is a psychiatric condition where concern about a very minor (or imagined) flaw is clearly excessive — sufferers may avoid leaving the house and strongly seek cosmetic dental work (whitening, facade work, orthodontics). The dentist should remain vigilant and practice restraint with unusual esthetic requests rather than simply providing the treatment.
